A2.stem: What two prices form the "body" of a single candlestick?
options: High and Low prices
Open and Close prices
Open and High prices
Close and Low prices
A2.explanation: The body is formed by the open and close prices; the high and low prices correspond to the endpoints of the wicks, not the body boundaries.

A2.stem: Under Midas' color convention, a candlestick with a "close higher than open" belongs to?
options: Bearish candle, green
Bullish candle, red
Bullish candle, green
Bearish candle, red
A2.explanation: Midas follows the "Red for Rise, Green for Fall" convention: close higher than open is a Bullish candle and red; close lower than open is a Bearish candle and green.

A3.stem: What does a longer "lower wick" on a candlestick mainly reflect?
options: Strong selling pressure above
Buying support below, price pulled back
Price will definitely rise next
Volume must expand
A3.explanation: The lower wick is the trace of price being pulled back after dropping; it reflects buying support below; "definitely rise" is a wrong certainty.

A3.stem: Which statement about wick length is correct?
options: The longer the wick, the more intense the battle between long and short
The longer the wick, the more stable the price
A long wick means a reversal is guaranteed
Wick length has no meaning
A3.explanation: A longer wick represents more intense fighting and confusion in direction at that time; it is a signal of the battle, not a guarantee of reversal.

options: When price rises
When price falls
When price is stagnant
Profitable in any situation
A4.explanation: Shorting is selling first and buying later; profit occurs only when price falls, loss when it rises; there is no situation where it is profitable in all directions.

A4.stem: Why can contracts facilitate shorting, while spot trading is mainly for Long?
options: Because spot is riskier so shorting is banned
Contracts support dual-direction (open Short), spot generally requires holding assets first
Because shorting is illegal
Because spot cannot make money
A4.explanation: Contracts are designed to support opening Shorts and dual-direction operations; spot generally requires holding/borrowing assets first, so it is mainly for Long.

A5.stem: What is the most accurate meaning of "Leverage"?
options: Using small margin to operate a large position
Borrowing for free to earn profit
A tool that guarantees profit
A tool that improves win rate
A5.explanation: Leverage uses small margin to leverage a large position; it does not improve win rate or guarantee profit, only amplifies results.

A5.stem: Which statement about leverage's impact on profit/loss is correct?
options: Amplifies profit only, not loss
Amplifies profit and loss equally
Amplifies loss only, not profit
Has no impact on profit/loss
A5.explanation: Leverage is a double-edged sword—it amplifies gains while equally amplifying losses, which is its essence to be wary of.

A5.stem: What consequence does higher leverage bring?
options: Safer, more resistant to volatility
Worse resistance to volatility, easier to Liquidate
Guarantees profit
Completely unrelated to Liquidation
A5.explanation: Higher leverage means smaller opposite fluctuations can wipe out margin and trigger forced Liquidation.

A6.stem: What does a "Support Level" refer to?
options: Area of selling pressure above the price
Area of buying pressure below the price, price tends to stop falling here
A price that will never be broken
A price set by the exchange
A6.explanation: Support is an area below price where buying pressure gathers and price tends to stop falling and rebound; it is not an absolute iron law.

A6.stem: After a resistance level is "broken upward" by price, what usually happens?
options: Disappears completely and becomes meaningless
Role reverses and often becomes a Support level
Becomes a stronger resistance level
Causes price to definitely rise
A6.explanation: Support and resistance transform with the direction of the breakout: a resistance broken upward often becomes support; "definitely rise" is a wrong certainty.

A6.stem: What is the correct understanding of Support and Resistance?
options: They are iron laws that must take effect
They are probabilistic reference areas, price may rebound or break through
They can precisely predict future price
Buy or sell immediately when price arrives
A6.explanation: Support and resistance are probabilistic reference areas that can fail; use them combined with other information; they do not predict price, nor are they trading orders.

A7.stem: What are the typical characteristics of an "uptrend" in K-line structure?
options: Higher highs and higher lows
Lower highs and lower lows
Highs and lows remain roughly flat
Price remains stagnant for a long time
A7.explanation: An uptrend is characterized by higher highs and higher lows (like climbing stairs); lower highs and lower lows indicate a downtrend.

A7.stem: Which of the following situations belongs to "consolidation (sideways)"?
options: Highs and lows remain roughly flat, price moves back and forth within a range with unclear direction
Higher highs and higher lows
Lower highs and lower lows
Price moves in a single direction and rises rapidly
A7.explanation: Consolidation is characterized by roughly flat highs and lows, price moving back and forth within a range with unclear direction, distinguishing it from single-direction uptrends or downtrends.

A8.stem: What is the core characteristic of a "Market Order"?
options: Executed immediately at the current market price, but price is not fully controllable (slippage may occur)
Executed only when the specified price is reached, may not execute
Guaranteed execution at the best price
Slippage will never occur
A8.explanation: Market orders prioritize "timeliness"—execution is immediate, but the execution price is not fully controllable and slippage may occur.

A8.stem: What is the core characteristic of a "Limit Order"?
options: Executed immediately at the market price
Placed at a specified price, executed only when the price is reached, may not execute
Guaranteed to execute regardless of the situation
Executes faster than a market order
A8.explanation: Limit orders prioritize "price"—placed at a specified price, executed only when the price is reached, price is controllable but execution is not guaranteed.

A9.stem: When going Long, where should the stop-loss price typically be set?
options: Above the entry price
Below the entry price
Exactly the same as the entry price
Anywhere is fine
A9.explanation: For Long positions, the stop-loss is set below the entry price—when the price drops to this level, the position is closed to control the single loss and prevent it from expanding.

A9.stem: Which of the following statements about stop-loss is correct?
options: Stop-loss guarantees final profit
Stop-loss prevents small losses from becoming large losses; it is risk control (but does not guarantee profit)
Stop-loss will cause you to miss all profits
As long as a stop-loss is set, losses will never occur
A9.explanation: The core of a stop-loss is "preventing small losses from becoming large losses"; it is a form of risk control rather than a guarantee of profit, and the actual exit price may deviate under extreme market conditions.

A10.stem: What is a significant characteristic of the A-share market compared to the cryptocurrency market?
options: A-shares implement T+1 and have price limits
A-shares trade 7×24 hours
A-shares have no price limits
A-shares are primarily short-selling
A10.explanation: A-shares implement T+1 and have price limits (e.g., ±10% on the main board), have high barriers for short selling, and are primarily long-selling; 7×24 trading and no price limits are characteristics of the crypto market.

A10.stem: What are the typical characteristics of the cryptocurrency market?
options: Trading opens for about 6.5 hours a day
7×24 hour trading, high volatility, no price limits
Fixed price limits are set
Short selling is completely impossible
A10.explanation: The crypto market operates 7×24 hours, has high volatility, and has no price limits; contracts are bidirectional and T+0. The rules differ significantly between markets; actual rules should be based on the latest official information.

A11.stem: One of the core differences between Spot and Futures (Perpetual) is?
options: Spot has leverage, Futures does not
Futures have leverage, are bidirectional, and carry liquidation risk; Spot has no leverage or liquidation risk by default
They are exactly the same
Spot risk is higher than Futures
A11.explanation: Futures have leverage, are bidirectional, and carry funding rates and liquidation risks, making the risk significantly higher; Spot involves buying and holding assets with no leverage or liquidation risk by default.

A11.stem: What does the "Funding Rate" in Perpetual Futures refer to?
options: The trading fee charged by the exchange
A mechanism unique to Perpetual Futures, periodically settled between longs and shorts
Bank deposit interest
Spot custody fee
A11.explanation: The funding rate is a mechanism unique to Perpetual Futures, periodically settled between longs and shorts (not a fee paid to the platform), often used to gauge market sentiment.

A11.stem: Midas Crypto focuses on "Futures Analysis" but adheres to the principle of?
options: Promising that users will definitely make money using futures
Fully virtual, AI analysis is for reference only and does not constitute investment advice
Providing real orders to help users make money
Guaranteeing prediction accuracy
A11.explanation: Midas is fully virtual; all analysis and AI are for reference only and do not constitute investment advice—no promise of profit is made, and price predictions are not provided.

options: Experience trading with simulated funds, with no real profit or loss involved
Practice with small amounts of real money
A strategy that guarantees steady profits
Only view market data without placing orders
A12.explanation: Virtual trading uses simulated funds to experience the full trading process without real profit or loss; its value lies in trial and error with zero real risk.

A12.stem: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the "proper use" of virtual trading?
options: Since no real money is lost, you can click randomly
Follow a serious "Learn → Practice → Review" loop and treat virtual trading like a real account
Treat it only as a game for entertainment
Virtual practice guarantees you can make money in the real market
A12.explanation: The proper use is a serious "Learn → Practice → Review" loop and treating virtual trading like a real account; however, doing well in virtual trading does not guarantee profitability in the real market.

B1.stem: What does the "5-Day Moving Average (MA5)" represent?
options: The average of closing prices over the last 5 periods, connected into a line
The highest price of the last 5 days
A prediction of prices for the next 5 days
The sum of trading volume over 5 periods
B1.explanation: Moving averages are the average of closing prices over the last N periods, calculated and connected into a line; they reflect past trends, not future predictions.

B1.stem: Which statement about the direction of moving averages is correct?
options: Moving averages can predict future prices
Moving averages reflect past trends: upward for bullish, downward for bearish
Short-term moving averages are always more useful than long-term ones
The direction of moving averages is unrelated to trends
B1.explanation: The direction of moving averages reflects trends (upward bullish, downward bearish, flat consolidation), but they reflect past trends, not future predictions; periods are not inherently better or worse.

B2.stem: What does the "Golden Cross" of moving averages refer to?
options: The long-term moving average crosses above the short-term moving average
The short-term moving average crosses above the long-term moving average
The price crosses above the moving average
Both moving averages move upward simultaneously
B2.explanation: Golden Cross = Short-term MA crosses above Long-term MA (bullish reference); do not reverse the direction; "Long crossing Short" actually corresponds to a Death Cross.

B2.stem: What does the "Death Cross" of moving averages refer to?
options: The short-term moving average crosses below the long-term moving average
The short-term moving average crosses above the long-term moving average
The price hits a new high
Trading volume increases significantly
B2.explanation: Death Cross = Short-term MA crosses below Long-term MA (bearish reference), opposite to the Golden Cross.

B2.stem: Which statement about the nature of Golden Cross and Death Cross is correct?
options: They are leading and precise buy/sell signals
They are lagging signals; by the time they appear, the price has often moved, and there are many false signals in consolidation
A Golden Cross means you should buy immediately
They are always accurate
B2.explanation: Golden Cross and Death Cross are lagging signals, with especially many false signals in consolidation; they are references, not predictions or trading orders, and cannot be traded solely based on them.

B3.stem: What is the correct order of a "Bullish Arrangement" from top to bottom?
options: Price > Short-term MA > Medium-term MA > Long-term MA
Long-term MA > Medium-term MA > Short-term MA > Price
Several moving averages are intertwined
Price is at the very bottom
B3.explanation: A bullish arrangement from top to bottom is Price > Short > Medium > Long (Short is on top, Price is at the top), representing a strong uptrend structure; the reverse is a bearish arrangement.

B3.stem: What market structure does a "Bearish Arrangement" represent?
options: Strong uptrend structure
Weak downtrend structure (Long > Medium > Short > Price, Price at the bottom)
It is definitely about to bottom out and rebound
It is unrelated to trend strength
B3.explanation: A bearish arrangement from top to bottom is Long > Medium > Short > Price, Price at the bottom, representing a weak downtrend structure; arrangement conversion is lagging and serves only as a reference.

B4.stem: What is the MACD "Red/Green Bar" equal to?
options: DIF − DEA
Fast MA − Slow MA
Closing Price − Opening Price
DEA − DIF
B4.explanation: Red/Green Bar = DIF − DEA: DIF above is positive (Red, above zero axis), below is negative (Green, below zero axis); where the two lines intersect, the bar is zero.

B4.stem: How is the DEA (Slow Line) in MACD derived?
options: The moving average of closing prices
The moving average of DIF, smoother and lagging behind DIF
The moving average of trading volume
Highest price minus lowest price
B4.explanation: DEA is the moving average of DIF (commonly 9), smoother than DIF and lagging behind it; while DIF = Fast MA − Slow MA.

B5.stem: What does a "MACD Golden Cross" refer to?
options: Short-term MA crosses above long-term MA
DIF crosses above DEA
Price crosses above the zero line
Red bars lengthen
B5.explanation: MACD Golden Cross = DIF crosses above DEA (bars turn from green to red); the protagonists are the DIF and DEA lines, not moving averages—"Short-term MA crosses above long-term MA" is a moving average golden cross.

B5.stem: What does a "MACD Death Cross" refer to?
options: DIF crosses below DEA
DEA crosses below DIF
Short-term MA crosses below long-term MA
Green bars shorten
B5.explanation: MACD Death Cross = DIF crosses below DEA (bars turn from red to green); it is a bearish reference; it is a crossover between DIF/DEA, not a moving average crossover.

B5.stem: What does the shortening of MACD red and green bars usually indicate?
options: Momentum strengthens
Momentum weakens
Price must reverse
Trend must end
B5.explanation: Bars lengthening = momentum strengthens; bars shortening = momentum weakens. The shortening of red bars often indicates the exhaustion of upward momentum, but does not equal a price reversal.

B6.stem: What is the "Top Divergence" of MACD?
options: Price makes a new high, but the MACD high actually drops
Price makes a new high, and the MACD high also rises synchronously
Price makes a new low, but the MACD high drops
Price and MACD fall in the same direction
B6.explanation: Top Divergence = Price highs rise (make new highs) but MACD highs drop (opposite direction), indicating exhaustion of upward momentum; the directional relationship must not be reversed.

B6.stem: What is the correct understanding of MACD divergence?
options: It is an exact timing tool that reverses immediately upon appearance
It indicates "possible reversal," but can be flat, persist, or fail; it does not predict timing or magnitude
It is always accurate
It is a clear buy or sell order
B6.explanation: Divergence indicates momentum exhaustion and "possible reversal," but it is not an exact timing tool—it can be flat, persist, or fail; it must be combined with context and risk management.

B7.stem: How are the "Upper and Lower Bands" of Bollinger Bands calculated?
options: Middle Band ± K times Standard Deviation (commonly K=2)
Middle Band ± Fixed Points
Highest price and lowest price over a period
Middle Band ± K times Volume
B7.explanation: Upper and Lower Bands = Middle Band ± K times Standard Deviation (commonly K=2), symmetrically distributed on either side of the Middle Band; Standard Deviation reflects volatility, so the channel "breathes."

B7.stem: What is the "Middle Band" of Bollinger Bands?
options: A Moving Average (commonly 20-period)
Highest price over a period
Previous day's closing price
Standard Deviation itself
B7.explanation: The Middle Band is a Moving Average (commonly 20-period), with the Upper and Lower Bands adding and subtracting the Standard Deviation on either side.

B7.stem: What is the correct understanding when price touches the Bollinger Band "Upper Band"?
options: Price must reverse and fall
This is a positional reference, not a reversal signal (price can run along the band in strong trends)
Must sell immediately
The channel must immediately close
B7.explanation: Touching the Upper or Lower Band is only a positional reference, not a reversal signal. In strong trends, price can run along the band, and it does not constitute a buy or sell order.

B8.stem: What does a "Bollinger Band Squeeze" mean?
options: Volatility increases
Volatility converges (Upper and Lower bands narrow, Standard Deviation decreases)
Price must fall
Trend must reverse
B8.explanation: Squeeze = Upper and Lower bands narrow, Standard Deviation decreases, volatility converges; a long squeeze is often seen as "brewing for a breakout."

B8.stem: What usually happens after a long period of "Bollinger Band Squeeze"?
options: Must break out upwards
Must break out downwards
Often welcomes a directional breakout, but the direction cannot be predicted
Price will never move
B8.explanation: A squeeze indicates a "volatility state" rather than direction. It is often followed by a directional breakout, but the direction is unpredictable and does not equal a guaranteed rise or fall.

B9.stem: What is the value range and midline of the RSI indicator?
options: 0–100, 50 as the midline
-100 to 100, 0 as the midline
0–10, 5 as the midline
No fixed range
B9.explanation: RSI takes values 0–100, with 50 as the midline; above 50 favors the uptrend, below 50 favors the downtrend.

B9.stem: What does it mean when RSI enters the "Overbought Zone" (often referenced as >70)?
options: Price will fall immediately, should sell
It is a reference for strength dominance, but does not mean falling immediately (can be flat in strong trends)
Price must peak
Must reverse immediately
B9.explanation: Overbought is a "reference zone"; Overbought ≠ falling immediately. In strong trends, RSI can be flat and stay at extreme values for a long time. It is not a reversal signal or a sell order.

B9.stem: What threshold is commonly used as a reference for the RSI "Oversold Zone"?
B9.explanation: Overbought is often referenced as >70, and Oversold is often referenced as <30 (thresholds are not unique); similarly, Oversold ≠ rising immediately.

C1.stem: Chan Theory decomposes price action using geometric structures. What is the order of structure from small to large?
options: Central Hub → Segment → Stroke → Fractal
Fractal → Stroke → Segment → Central Hub
Stroke → Fractal → Central Hub → Segment
MA → MACD → Central Hub → Trend
C1.explanation: Chan Theory structure from small to large: Fractal → Stroke → Segment → Central Hub, and possesses the characteristic of recursive levels.

C1.stem: Regarding Chan Theory, which of the following perceptions is rational and correct?
options: It is a divine tool that can predict future tops and bottoms
It is a tool that analyzes price action using strict geometric structures; it has a learning curve, is not deified, and does not guarantee steady profits
Mastering Chan Theory guarantees steady profits
It is more accurate than all analysis methods
C1.explanation: Chan Theory is an analysis tool, not a divine tool for prediction; the system is vast and has a threshold, and it does not promise steady profits.

C2.stem: Before learning Chan Theory, what is the most important mindset to establish?
options: Treat it as a holy grail that can predict tops and bottoms
Treat it as an analysis tool, focus on understanding structure rather than memorizing formulas, and always combine it with risk management
Use it to find 'sure-to-rise' signals and then go all-in
Believe that the more esoteric it is, the more accurate it is
C2.explanation: Chan Theory is an analysis tool, not a holy grail; you must understand structure and combine it with risk management, rather than memorizing formulas to find sure-to-rise signals.

C2.stem: Which of the following tendencies belongs to the 'going crazy' (obsession) to watch out for when learning Chan Theory?
options: Understanding the logic behind the structure
Deifying and esotericizing Chan Theory, and 'using it to predict and then going all-in'
Learning step-by-step in order
Always combining it with risk management
C2.explanation: Be wary of tendencies to deify/esotericize/faith-based Chan Theory, as well as the tendency to 'use it to predict and go all-in'.

C3.stem: The first step in Chan Theory is to handle the 'Inclusion Relationship' of K-lines. What is the purpose?
options: To make the price go up
To eliminate structural ambiguity and make tops and bottoms clear, facilitating the identification of Fractals and drawing Strokes
To predict price direction
To increase trading volume
C3.explanation: Handling the inclusion relationship is to eliminate structural ambiguity and make tops and bottoms clear; it is the prerequisite basic skill for identifying Fractals and drawing Strokes.

C3.stem: What is the rule for handling K-line inclusion relationships?
options: Always take the higher one
For upward movement, take the 'higher-high' and 'higher-low'; for downward movement, take the 'lower-low' and 'lower-high'; the direction is determined by the direction of the previous K-line
Always take the average of the two
Directly delete one of them
C3.explanation: For upward movement, take the 'higher-high' and 'higher-low'; for downward movement, take the 'lower-low' and 'lower-high'; the direction is determined by the previous K-line.

C4.stem: Which of the following descriptions fits a 'Top Fractal'?
options: The high point and low point of the middle K-line are the highest (overall highest)
The middle K-line is overall the lowest
The three K-lines are equally high
The first K-line is the highest
C4.explanation: Top Fractal = the middle K-line is overall the highest (both high and low points are highest); the Bottom Fractal is the opposite, being the middle K-line overall the lowest.

C4.stem: How many K-lines constitute a Fractal?
options: Two
Three (adjacent K-lines after handling inclusion relationships)
Five
One
C4.explanation: A Fractal is composed of three adjacent K-lines after handling inclusion relationships, marking a local reversal.

C4.stem: Regarding the significance of Fractals, which of the following perceptions is correct?
options: The appearance of a Fractal represents a major trend reversal
Fractals only mark local reversals and are endpoints for drawing Strokes; they do not represent a major trend reversal and cannot be used for prediction
When a Top Fractal appears, you should sell
Fractals can predict subsequent rises and falls
C4.explanation: Fractals only mark local reversals and are endpoints for drawing Strokes; they do not represent a major trend reversal, cannot predict, and are not trading signals.

C5.stem: What does a Stroke represent in Chan Theory?
options: A single K-line
Connecting an adjacent Top Fractal and Bottom Fractal
A Moving Average
The boundary of a Central Hub
C5.explanation: Stroke = connecting an adjacent Top Fractal and Bottom Fractal; it is the most basic unit of price action.

C5.stem: Regarding the direction of a Stroke, which of the following statements is correct?
options: Multiple consecutive Strokes can be in the same direction
Stroke directions alternate up and down (Up Stroke = Bottom Fractal → Top Fractal, Down Stroke = Top Fractal → Bottom Fractal); consecutive same-direction Strokes do not occur
Strokes are always upward
Stroke direction is random
C5.explanation: Stroke directions alternate up and down: Up Stroke = Bottom Fractal → Top Fractal, Down Stroke = Top Fractal → Bottom Fractal; consecutive same-direction Strokes do not occur.

E6.stem: What aspect of the market does the Long/Short Ratio reflect?
options: Price fluctuation magnitude
Ratio of Long to Short positions (Holding bias/Mood)
Volume size
Funding rate level
E6.explanation: Long/Short Ratio = Ratio of Long to Short positions, reflecting participants' holding bias and sentiment distribution.

E6.stem: Which of the following understandings about the Long/Short Ratio is correct?
options: If Longs are many, price will definitely rise
It has different metrics, is a sentiment reference, does not predict, and is not a signal
It can precisely predict price direction
The rule 'If Longs are many, look for a short' is reliable
E6.explanation: Long/Short ratios use different samples, such as top traders or account counts. They describe positioning sentiment; neither “more longs means price must rise” nor a fixed contrarian rule is reliable.

E7.stem: Which is the calculation method for Basis?
options: Spot Price - Perpetual Price
Perpetual Price - Spot Price
Highest Price - Lowest Price
Bid Price - Ask Price
E7.explanation: Basis = Perpetual Price - Spot Price; Positive Basis = Premium (expensive), Negative Basis = Discount (cheap).

E7.stem: Which of the following statements about the relationship between Basis and Funding Rate is correct?
options: They have no relation
Premium is often accompanied by positive funding, Discount by negative funding; the funding rate is the 'hand' pulling the Perpetual price back to Spot
Premium is always accompanied by negative funding
Basis can precisely predict price
E7.explanation: Basis is highly correlated with the direction of funding (Premium -> Positive Funding); the funding rate anchors the Perpetual price to Spot. Basis is a reference, not a prediction.

E8.stem: What is the most appropriate understanding of calling a contract a 'double-edged sword'?
options: Leverage only amplifies profit
Leverage amplifies both ways—amplifying gains while equally amplifying losses, and risk of Liquidation
Contracts are actually risk-free
Contracts have no risk
E8.explanation: Leverage amplifies gains and losses both ways, with the risk of Liquidation (principal may go to zero), which is the meaning of 'double-edged sword'.

E8.stem: Besides amplifying gains and losses, what else does a contract amplify?
options: Only amplifies principal, does not affect others
It also amplifies emotional and behavioral risks (impulse, overtrading, gambling nature), often hurting more than a single loss
It will amplify your win rate
Nothing is amplified additionally
E8.explanation: Contracts also amplify emotional and behavioral risks, often hurting more than a single loss, so beginners must be extra cautious.

E9.stem: Among the many principles for preventing Liquidation, which is placed first?
options: Increase leverage to seek higher returns
Control leverage, start with low leverage (larger margin for error)
Operate with full position as much as possible
Do not set stop loss at all
E9.explanation: Controlling leverage (starting with low leverage) is the priority; it directly determines the size of the margin for error.

E9.stem: Where should the stop loss price be set to prevent Liquidation?
options: On the earlier (less extreme) side than the Liquidation price, to exit actively
Exactly equal to the Liquidation price
On the more extreme side than the Liquidation price
Stop loss is not needed at all
E9.explanation: Stop loss should be set on the earlier side than the Liquidation price for an active exit, rather than waiting for the market to force-close you.

E9.stem: What is the correct understanding of these Liquidation prevention principles?
options: Following them guarantees no Liquidation
They reduce risk but do not eliminate risk; no method guarantees 'no Liquidation'
With a stop loss, you definitely profit
Sufficient margin allows you to predict the market
E9.explanation: These are cumulative habits to reduce risk, not a promise that 'following them is safe'; reducing risk ≠ eliminating risk.

E10.stem: Midas's contract analysis is 'fully virtual'; its greatest value lies in?
options: Using a virtual account to earn real money
Understanding and practicing high-risk contracts (including making mistakes and Liquidation) with zero real risk
Guaranteeing you will profit after learning
Helping you predict price
E10.explanation: Fully virtual = building risk awareness and practicing contracts with zero real risk; it does not promise profit and does not predict price.

E10.stem: What is the correct attitude towards Midas's AI contract analysis?
options: Treat it as precise buy/sell instructions to follow
For reference only, does not constitute investment advice, does not predict price
It guarantees accuracy
It promises profit
E10.explanation: AI analysis is for reference only, does not constitute investment advice, and does not predict price; no analysis dimension guarantees accuracy or promises profit.

E1.stem: A trader wants to hold a crypto contract position long-term without rolling over at expiration. Which tool best fits this need?
options: Traditional Delivery Futures
Perpetual
Options
Spot DCA
E1.explanation: Perpetual contracts have no expiration date, allow long-term holding, and require no rolling over; traditional delivery futures have expiration dates and require rolling over, making them unsuitable for the 'no rolling over' requirement.

E1.stem: What is the core difference between Perpetual and traditional futures?
options: Perpetual has no leverage
Perpetual cannot Short
Perpetual has no expiration date and is pegged to spot via funding rates
Perpetual has no risk
E1.explanation: Perpetuals have no expiration date and are pegged to spot via funding rates; traditional futures have expiration dates and converge to spot upon expiration. Perpetuals also have leverage, allow for both directions, and carry risk.

E2.stem: A perpetual contract currently shows a 'Positive Funding Rate'. What does this mean for this settlement cycle?
options: Short pays Long
Long pays Short
Exchange pays all holders
Everyone pays Exchange
E2.explanation: Positive funding rate = Long pays Short; Negative funding rate = Short pays Long (direction must never be reversed).

E2.stem: Regarding the nature of funding rates, which statement is correct?
options: It is the transaction fee charged by the exchange
It is a periodic payment between Longs and Shorts to peg the Perpetual price to spot
It is the loan interest paid to the bank
It is the platform's profit source
E2.explanation: Funding is a transfer between Longs and Shorts, not a fee paid to the platform; it settles periodically to keep the Perpetual price close to spot.

E2.stem: Regarding the function of funding rates, which perception is correct?
options: High rates definitely mean the price will rise
It serves as sentiment reference but does not predict price, and the paid funding is a holding cost
Funding can precisely predict the direction of price movement
Funding paid during long-term holding is not considered a cost
E2.explanation: Funding rates serve as sentiment reference but do not predict price; the continuous funding paid during long-term holding is a tangible holding cost.

E3.stem: Which description fits the 'Isolated' margin mode?
options: Using the entire account balance to backstop the position
Each position uses independent margin; liquidation only risks losing that position's margin
Never subject to forced liquidation
Risk is definitely higher than Cross
E3.explanation: Isolated risk isolation means liquidation risks only the margin of that specific position, not other funds; using the full balance to backstop is Cross.

E3.stem: Regarding the choice between Cross and Isolated, which perception is correct?
options: Choosing Isolated means no liquidation risk
Both modes have liquidation risk; choosing one only changes risk distribution, it does not eliminate risk
Cross mode guarantees profit
Choosing the right mode guarantees profit
E3.explanation: Both modes carry liquidation risk, only the distribution of risk differs; both require leverage and position size control.

E4.stem: A trader opened a 'Long' order. Where is its liquidation price located?
options: Above the entry price
Below the entry price
At the entry price
No liquidation price
E4.explanation: The liquidation price for a Long is below the entry price, and for a Short it is above (direction must never be reversed).

E4.stem: All else equal, the higher the leverage, how does the liquidation price change?
options: Further from entry price, safer
Closer to entry price, easier to be triggered
Unrelated to leverage level
Completely disappears
E4.explanation: Leverage is the most critical factor affecting liquidation price: the higher the leverage, the closer the liquidation price is to the entry price, leaving less room for error.

E4.stem: Why does actual liquidation often happen earlier than the 'theoretical liquidation price' calculated by the formula?
options: The exchange deliberately liquidates early to scam users
Because of the maintenance margin rate, plus fees, funding, and slippage, liquidation is triggered before 'losing everything'
Because the price is calculated incorrectly
It does not actually happen earlier
E4.explanation: The maintenance margin rate requires margin not to fall below a certain level; combined with various fees, actual liquidation often occurs before the theoretical price of 'zero margin'.

options: Total transaction volume for the day
Total volume of outstanding contracts in the market (stock)
Price levels
Ratio of Longs to Shorts
E5.explanation: OI = Total outstanding contracts, it is a 'stock', distinct from trading volume which is a 'flow'.

E5.stem: When OI increases significantly, what does it usually mean? Which statement is correct?
options: Position increase, new capital entering (but OI is a reference, not a prediction, not a signal)
Price will definitely rise
Capital is leaving in large amounts
The market has definitely peaked
E5.explanation: OI increase = Position increase (new capital entering); however, it is only a reference dimension and does not predict price or serve as an operational signal.

C6.stem: What is the core requirement for a Segment to be established?
options: At least three consecutive Strokes, and the Strokes must overlap
Any two Strokes are sufficient
A single very long candle
Gather five Fractals
C6.explanation: A Segment requires at least three consecutive Strokes, and the Strokes must overlap (e.g., the price overlap area between the first and third upward Strokes).

C6.stem: What is the relationship between the levels of a Segment and a Stroke?
options: The Stroke is one level higher than the Segment
The Segment is one level higher than the Stroke (Strokes constitute Segments, reflecting recursive levels)
They are the same level
They are unrelated
C6.explanation: The Segment is one level higher than the Stroke and is smoother and more stable; Strokes constitute Segments, reflecting the recursive levels of Chan Theory.

C7.stem: What does the 'Central Hub' (Zhongshu) in Chan Theory refer to?
options: A single candle
The overlapping interval of three consecutive lower-level trends
The range from the highest price to the lowest price
A Moving Average
C7.explanation: A Central Hub is the overlapping interval of three consecutive lower-level trends; the three trends must have a common overlap, otherwise, it is not a Central Hub.

C7.stem: Regarding the upper and lower boundaries of a Central Hub, which value is correct?
options: Upper boundary = the highest of the three high points, Lower boundary = the lowest of the three low points
Upper boundary = the lowest of the three high points, Lower boundary = the highest of the three low points
Upper boundary = the overall highest price, Lower boundary = the overall lowest price
Upper and lower boundaries can be chosen arbitrarily
C7.explanation: The upper boundary of a Central Hub is the minimum of the three high points, and the lower boundary is the maximum of the three low points (i.e., the boundaries of the common overlapping area of the three trends). They must not be reversed.

C7.stem: What market state does the essence of a Central Hub reflect?
options: A clear unilateral trend
A volatile area of long/short balance (often corresponding to consolidation)
A position of inevitable reversal
A clear buy signal
C7.explanation: A Central Hub is a volatile area of long/short balance, often corresponding to consolidation; it has levels, forms, extends, and generates new ones.

C8.stem: Regarding the 'Three Types of Buy/Sell Points' in Chan Theory, what is the most important and most essential cognition?
options: Buy when a buy point appears and sell when a sell point appears
It is a term describing structural positions, not trading instructions; it does not predict, guarantee, or constitute investment advice
Buy/Sell points will definitely materialize
Buy/Sell points can precisely predict tops and bottoms
C8.explanation: Buy/Sell points are terms describing structural positions, not trading instructions; they can fail and depend on subjective judgment, so they must be combined with risk management.

C8.stem: What structural position does the First Type of Buy Point describe?
options: Any position during an uptrend
The turning low point at the end of a downtrend, where the last downward segment diverges from the previous segment (momentum exhaustion)
The position of breaking a new high
Any low point
C8.explanation: The First Type of Buy Point is the turning low point at the end of a downtrend after a Divergence (momentum exhaustion).

C8.stem: What structural position does the Third Type of Buy Point describe?
options: The price pulls back after breaking upward through the Central Hub, without falling back into the Central Hub (not breaking the upper boundary)
The position where the price breaks through the Central Hub
The position where the price moves back and forth inside the Central Hub
The position where the price creates a new low
C8.explanation: The Third Type of Buy Point is the pullback after breaking upward through the Central Hub, where the pullback does not fall back into the Central Hub (not breaking the upper boundary).

C9.stem: Regarding the limitations of Chan Theory, which statement is correct?
options: Chan Theory can precisely predict and has no limitations
It has ambiguity (classification is subjective), lag (based on past trends), and requires combination with other analysis
Chan Theory can independently determine all operations
Chan Theory has no lag at all
C9.explanation: Chan Theory has ambiguity and lag and requires combination with other analysis; it is a 'mirror to see structure,' not a 'crystal ball to foresee the future.'

C9.stem: What is the reasonable use of Chan Theory?
options: Mechanically applying Buy/Sell points and pursuing absolute precision
Structurally understanding trends, assisting in judging current positions, and placing them in a complete system combined with risk management
Treating it as a prediction artifact and trading heavily
Believing that the more mysterious it is, the better
C9.explanation: Reasonable use = structurally understanding trends, assisting in judgment, and combining with risk management; beware of mechanical application, excessive pursuit of precision, and mythologizing the theory.

F2.stem: What is the core significance of 'Plan first, trade later'?
options: To make trading more frequent
Use pre-trade rationality to counter emotions during holding
Guaranteeing profit on every trade
Used to predict prices
F2.explanation: The trading plan moves decision-making to a 'calm time,' using pre-trade rationality to counter emotions during holding.

F2.stem: Regarding the separation of 'Planning and Execution', what is the correct approach?
options: Modify the plan arbitrarily based on feelings while holding
In the execution phase, follow the plan strictly and do not change it temporarily (especially do not move stops arbitrarily)
Simply do not write a plan and trade directly
Move the stop loss back every time you incur a loss
F2.explanation: In the execution phase, follow the plan strictly and do not change your mind temporarily, especially do not move stops arbitrarily while holding.

F3.stem: What is the calculation for Risk-Reward Ratio (Profit-Loss Ratio)?
options: Win Rate ÷ Loss
Potential Profit ÷ Potential Loss
Profit × Win Rate
Volume Ratio
F3.explanation: Profit-Loss Ratio = Potential Profit ÷ Potential Loss, determined by entry, stop loss, and take profit.

F3.stem: Regarding 'Win Rate' and 'Profit-Loss Ratio', which statement is correct?
options: Higher win rate always means more profit
Relying solely on win rate leads to misjudgment: 40% win rate + 1:2 ratio may profit, while 70% win rate but poor ratio may also lose
Profit-Loss Ratio is irrelevant
Only 100% win rate leads to profit
F3.explanation: Relying solely on win rate leads to misjudgment; it must be viewed in conjunction with the profit-loss ratio. Low win rate + high ratio can still be profitable overall.

F3.stem: When the profit-loss ratio is 1:2, what is the approximate 'Break-even Win Rate'?
options: Approximately 50%
Approximately 33%
Approximately 25%
Approximately 70%
F3.explanation: The higher the profit-loss ratio, the lower the required break-even win rate: 1:1 is approx 50%, 1:2 is approx 33%, 1:3 is approx 25%.

F4.stem: What primarily determines how long you can 'survive in the market'?
options: Luck of individual trades
Position sizing
The higher the leverage, the better
How accurate your predictions are
F4.explanation: Individual trade outcomes depend on the market, but long-term survival depends mainly on position sizing.

F4.stem: In the 'Fixed Percentage Risk Method (e.g., 1%)', what does the '1%' refer to?
options: Position size is 1% of total capital
Maximum loss of total capital at stop loss
Trading only 1% of the time per day
Leverage is 1%
F4.explanation: '1%' refers to the 'maximum loss percentage at stop loss', not the position percentage.

F4.stem: How should position size be determined?
options: Based on gut feeling
Position = Risk Amount ÷ Stop Loss Distance (Stop loss wider = smaller position)
The bigger, the better
Equal to the entire account balance
F4.explanation: Use stop loss to reverse-calculate position size to ensure constant single-trade risk; the wider the stop loss, the smaller the position, and vice versa.

F6.stem: What is the essence of trading 'Discipline'?
options: Trade as frequently as possible
Execute according to pre-set rules, do not change your mind based on emotions at the last minute
Operate entirely on intuition
Always stay fully positioned
F6.explanation: Discipline = executing according to established rules; doing what you must do and stopping when you must stop, not being swayed by on-the-spot emotions.

F6.stem: When the market has no opportunities that fit your system, what is the correct action?
options: Must always maintain a position
Not trading is also a correct operation (frequently looking for trades is overtrading and a breach of discipline)
Pick any target and make a trade
The more frequently you trade, the better
F6.explanation: Overtrading is a typical breach of discipline; not trading when there are no opportunities is itself a correct operation.

F8.stem: What is the core philosophy of a Trend Trading System?
options: Fishing for bottoms and tops, predicting turning points
Trade in the direction of the confirmed trend, do not guess the top or bottom
Buy as it falls, average down costs
Only trade back and forth within a range
F8.explanation: Trend trading = trading in the direction of the confirmed trend, not guessing tops and bottoms; only Long on upswings, only Short or avoid on downswings.

F8.stem: In which market conditions is a Trend Trading System most prone to repeated stop losses?
options: Trend market
Ranging market
Any market is the same
It will never stop loss
F8.explanation: Trend trading is prone to repeated stop losses in ranging markets; it has applicable market conditions, does not guarantee profit, and requires risk management.

F9.stem: What is the core approach of a Range Trading System?
options: Chase breakouts
Sell high and buy low within the range (buy near support, sell near resistance)
Hold single-directionly without moving
Add positions as it rises
F9.explanation: Range trading = selling high and buying low within the range, provided the market is indeed ranging.

F9.stem: What risk does a Range Trading System need to be most vigilant about?
options: Almost no risk
Fake breakouts and 'getting trapped at trend start' (breakout direction is unpredictable), thus relying heavily on strict stop loss
Guaranteed profit
Funding rate
F9.explanation: The two major risks are fake breakouts and getting trapped at trend start; the breakout direction is unpredictable, so range trading relies heavily on strict stop loss.

F12.stem: What is the P&L characteristic of trend following strategies (also the hardest part)?
options: High win rate, small profits on every trade
Win rate is often low, profits concentrated in a few major trends, requiring endurance of many small stop-losses
Never lose money
Win rate close to 100%
F12.explanation: Trend following has a low win rate, relies on a few major trends for profit, and requires enduring many small stop-losses; the difficulty lies in execution and mindset.

F12.stem: What is the correct understanding of the 'Turtle Trading Rules'?
options: Copying them now guarantees profit
It is a classic case of rule-based trend following, but the market has changed and past rules do not guarantee current effectiveness; it is for understanding the philosophy only
It is a holy grail for steady profits
It can predict tops and bottoms
F12.explanation: The Turtle Rules are for understanding the philosophy of rule-based trend following and cannot be copied blindly; past effectiveness does not imply future effectiveness.

F12.stem: What is the common practice of trend following?
options: Predict tops and bottoms, enter against the trend
Enter on breakouts or pullbacks in the trend direction, follow with a trailing stop, let profits run
Double down after a loss
Hold full position and refuse to stop loss
F12.explanation: Trend following = enter in trend direction + trailing stop + let profits run; do not predict tops and bottoms.

F13.stem: What is the essence of breakout trading?
options: Enter in the trend direction when price breaks a key level (belongs to trend-following/right-side approach)
Buy the dip against the trend at a low level
Buy high and sell low within a range
Double down after a loss
F13.explanation: Breakout trading = enter in the trend direction when price breaks a key level; its essence is a trend-following/right-side approach.

F13.stem: What is the biggest enemy of breakout strategies?
options: Funding rate
False breakouts (brief breakout then retracts)
Trend markets
Low volatility
F13.explanation: False breakouts are the biggest enemy; confirmation can be improved with volume, closing price stability, and pullback tests, but no method can 100% eliminate them.

F13.stem: After entering a breakout, where should the stop loss typically be placed?
options: On the other side of the key level (where the breakout is invalidated)
As far away as possible
No stop loss at all
At the profit target
F13.explanation: Place the stop loss on the other side of the key level; if the price retracts (breakout invalidated), execute a strict stop loss.

F14.stem: What is the relationship between mean reversion strategies and trend following strategies?
options: They are exactly the same
They are opposite worldviews (betting on reversion vs. betting on continuation), suitable for ranging/trend markets respectively
Both bet on trend continuation
They have no relationship
F14.explanation: Mean reversion bets on 'returning to the mean', while trend following bets on 'trend continuation'; they are opposite worldviews suitable for different market conditions.

F14.stem: Mean reversion strategies have a 'fatal premise'; what is it?
options: Must use leverage
The market must indeed be ranging; otherwise, if it is a trend, mean reversion against the trend will be crushed
Must trade with full position
Price will definitely return
F14.explanation: The fatal premise is that the market is indeed ranging; if a trend starts, you will be trapped, and the price may continue to deviate without guaranteeing a return (oversold can become more oversold).

F14.stem: What are the common tools used to measure 'how much price deviates from the mean'?
options: Volume
MA deviation, Bollinger Bands (deviation from upper/lower bands), RSI overbought/oversold
Open Interest (OI)
Long/Short ratio
F14.explanation: Common tools include MA deviation, Bollinger Bands, and RSI to measure deviation; enter against the trend when deviating, take profit when returning to the mean, and strictly stop loss if deviation continues.

F15.stem: What is the principle of grid trading?
options: Hold single-sidedly without moving
Layered orders within a range, mechanical buy high and sell low
Chase breakouts continuously
Predict tops and bottoms
F15.explanation: Grid = layered orders within a range, mechanical buy high and sell low, earning small profits from oscillations.

F15.stem: What is the fatal weakness of grid trading?
options: Ranging markets
Single-sided markets (single-sided down traps you deeper, single-sided up leaves you empty-handed; profit/loss asymmetry)
It has no weakness
Transaction fees
F15.explanation: The fatal weakness is single-sided markets, resulting in asymmetrical profit/loss (small wins, big losses); adding leverage to grid trading can lead to direct liquidation during single-sided moves, it is definitely not a 'lie flat and earn' strategy.

F15.stem: What is the correct understanding of 'Martingale' (doubling down after a loss)?
options: It is a method that never loses
It is more dangerous than grid trading: theoretically requires infinite capital, long-term almost inevitably encounters catastrophic drawdowns/liquidation, strongly not recommended
It has no risk
It is especially suitable for beginners
F15.explanation: Martingale requires infinite capital and almost inevitably leads to liquidation/bankruptcy in the long run; it is absolutely not a viable strategy and strongly not recommended.

F16.stem: Regarding the distinction between left-side and right-side trading, which of the following is correct?
options: Left side = enter after confirmation, Right side = layout in advance
Left side = layout before confirmation (against the trend), Right side = enter after confirmation (in the trend)
They are the same thing
Both are against-the-trend trading
F16.explanation: Left side = layout before confirmation (against the trend, bottom fishing/top picking), Right side = enter after confirmation (following the trend).

F16.stem: What is the correct understanding of 'bottom fishing'?
options: With the right method, you can precisely catch the bottom
Left-side bottom fishing is extremely risky during a decline; no method can precisely catch the bottom or top (tops and bottoms are only known after the fact)
Bottom fishing is steady profit
Can precisely predict turning points
F16.explanation: Left-side bottom fishing is extremely risky, cannot precisely catch bottoms or tops, and does not predict turning points; stop loss must be used regardless of left or right side.

F17.stem: What is the core meaning of "No Holy Grail"?
options: There exists a strongest strategy that profits in all market conditions
No strategy exists that can profit consistently in all markets and at all times
Finding the Holy Grail guarantees easy profits
Chan Theory is that Holy Grail
F17.explanation: No Holy Grail: Every strategy has applicable boundaries, and effectiveness decays over time.

F17.stem: Since there is no Holy Grail, what is the true core competency of trading?
options: Continuously searching for the strongest single strategy

Identifying market environment + using the right strategy in the right environment + using a complete system to compensate for the limitations of a single strategy (and accepting that identification can also be wrong)
Increasing leverage
Frequently switching strategies
F17.explanation: The core competency is identifying the environment, matching the strategy to the environment, using a system to compensate for limitations, and accepting that 'identifying the environment can also be wrong'.

F21.stem: What is the basic idea of funding rate arbitrage?
options: Longing with heavy single-side position to earn funding rates
Holding opposite-direction, equal-scale spot + contract positions to hedge directional risk and only earn funding rates
Chasing breakouts all the way
Doubling position size after a loss
F21.explanation: Funding rate arbitrage = Spot + Contract hedge (delta neutral), hedging directional risk to earn only funding rates.

F21.stem: What is the correct understanding of the risks of funding rate arbitrage?
options: It is true risk-free arbitrage
It swaps directional risk for a basket of risks: basis fluctuation, liquidation (fatal if contract leg is liquidated), reverse funding rates, costs, liquidity, etc.
It has absolutely no risk
It has huge returns and is risk-free
F21.explanation: Arbitrage is never risk-free; among the five major risks, liquidation of the contract leg is the most fatal; returns are thin while risks are real.

F21.stem: In a 'positive funding rate' market, how should one position to earn funding rates?
options: Hold contract Long to pay fees
Hold contract Short to earn fees, hedge direction with spot Long
Only do spot
Only do contract Long
F21.explanation: Positive funding rate = Long pays Short, therefore hold contract Short to earn fees and hedge direction with spot Long (practical implementation is more complex).

F22.stem: To protect existing spot Longs while fearing a short-term drop, what is the basic hedging structure?
options: Buy more spot
Spot Long + Contract Short (Short floating profit offsets Spot floating loss during a drop)
Spot Long + Contract Long
Directly close position
F22.explanation: Spot Long + Contract Short: During a drop, the Short floating profit offsets the Spot floating loss (protection); during a rise, profits are also hedged away (cost), essentially locking volatility.

F22.stem: What is the correct understanding of hedging/insurance?
options: Hedging eliminates all risk and has no cost
Hedging reduces directional risk but does not eliminate all risk, and has a cost (opportunity cost, funding rates, contract leg liquidation means insurance fails)
Hedging is a guaranteed profit
Hedging has no cost
F22.explanation: Hedging reduces directional risk but does not eliminate all risks; there is opportunity cost, funding rates, and if the contract leg is liquidated, the 'insurance' fails.

F23.stem: In contracts, how is profit and loss calculated?
options: Calculated based on margin usage
Calculated based on Notional Exposure (= Margin × Leverage)
Calculated based on account total
Calculated based on trading fees
F23.explanation: P&L is calculated based on Notional Exposure, not Margin; 'Only invest 1000, max loss 1000' is a fatal misconception.

F23.stem: How to correctly apply the 1% Risk Rule to contracts?
options: Maximize leverage first
Max loss per trade is 1% → Notional Exposure = Risk Amount ÷ Stop Loss Distance; Leverage only determines margin usage, not single-trade loss
Leverage directly determines single-trade loss
The larger the position, the better
F23.explanation: First determine 1% risk, then reverse-calculate Notional Exposure; Leverage only determines margin usage, not single-trade loss, so you cannot maximize leverage first.

F23.stem: What should be the relationship between leverage and stop loss to prevent liquidation?
options: The higher the leverage, the better
Use sufficiently low leverage to ensure the liquidation price is far from the stop loss price (ensuring the stop loss always triggers before liquidation)
Stop loss can be set after the liquidation price
Ignore leverage completely
F23.explanation: Excessive leverage leads to 'liquidation before stop loss', invalidating the 1% Risk Rule; use low leverage to ensure the liquidation price is far from the stop loss price.

F24.stem: What is the common core of these five errors: full position high leverage, holding positions without stop loss, ignoring funding rates, overtrading, treating contracts like a casino?
options: In contracts, these are all amplified by leverage into fatal wounds (contracts amplify the 'cost of mistakes')
They are all trivial issues
They are actually profitable
They are unrelated to leverage
F24.explanation: These errors may be minor issues in spot, but in contracts they are amplified by leverage into fatal wounds—contracts amplify the 'cost of mistakes'.

F24.stem: What is the most recommended way to avoid these contract practical errors?
options: Go straight to high leverage live trading to practice
First make these mistakes zero-cost in a virtual environment + discipline execution + respect for risk
Simply do not set a stop loss
The more frequent the trading, the better
F24.explanation: It is recommended to first make mistakes zero-cost in a virtual environment + discipline execution + respect for risk; corresponding discipline: low leverage, strict stop loss, position control, restraint from overtrading.

C1-6.stem: Regarding the 'level' of buy and sell points, which of the following is correct?
options: Buy and sell points have no distinction in level
The level of a buy or sell point is determined by the level of the Divergence that produced it; larger-level buy and sell points have stronger momentum than smaller-level ones
Smaller-level buy and sell points are definitely stronger
The level of a buy or sell point equals the daily time cycle
C1-6.explanation: Buy and sell point level = the level of the Divergence that produced it; the larger the level, the stronger the momentum and the larger the corresponding amplitude. Using smaller-level buy and sell points for large positions is a level mismatch.

C1-7.stem: When using MACD to judge 'Divergence', what is the main focus?
options: Red and green bar area expanding
Yellow and white lines (DIF/DEA) pullback + red and green bar area shrinking
Appearance of Golden cross
Price hitting a new high counts as Divergence
C1-7.explanation: Divergence is the exhaustion of momentum, judged by the yellow and white lines pullback + red and green bar area shrinking; bar area expansion is precisely an increase in momentum.

C1-7.stem: Regarding 'Divergence', which of the following understandings is correct?
options: Divergence will immediately reverse and top out with a guaranteed fall
Divergence is a reference for exhaustion of momentum in the same direction, not equal to an immediate reversal, and can stagnate
Divergence can precisely predict the timing of reversal
Divergence will definitely create a major move
C1-7.explanation: Divergence is only a reference for momentum exhaustion and does not equal an immediate reversal; it can stagnate in strong trends; further structural confirmation is required.

C1-8.stem: When looking at the Second Buy Point and Third Buy Point together, what is the difference in their 'personality'?
options: 2 Buy is on the left (early, cheap, low confirmation), 3 Buy is on the right (late, expensive, high confirmation)
2 Buy is on the right, 3 Buy is on the left
They are completely the same
2 Buy is definitely safer and more profitable than 3 Buy
C1-8.explanation: 2 Buy is on the left (near the bottom, early, cheap but low confirmation, high risk), 3 Buy is on the right (after breaking the Central Hub, late, expensive but high confirmation), corresponding to the trade-off between left and right.

C1-9.stem: Regarding the relationship between 'level' and 'time cycle (1m/5m/Daily)', which is correct?
options: Level is the time cycle, 5-minute level = 5-minute chart
Level is the size derived from the recursive structure of the trend, while the time cycle is the viewing scale of the chart; they can be related but cannot be equated
They have no relationship
The larger the level, the shorter the time cycle
C1-9.explanation: Level is the size derived from the recursive structure of the trend, while the cycle is just the viewing scale of the chart; multiple level structures can be nested within the same cycle chart; they can be approximated but are not equal.

C1-9.stem: What is the core approach of 'multi-level joint analysis'?
options: Large level determines direction and sets the range, small level finds the precise entry
Small level determines direction, large level finds the entry
Looking at just one level is enough
The more levels, the more accurate; just look at them all
C1-9.explanation: Joint analysis = large level determines direction, small level finds the entry (large level as primary, small level as auxiliary); each performs its own function.

C1-10.stem: Regarding 'level resonance' (multi-level same direction), which of the following understandings is correct?
options: Resonance = guaranteed profit, inevitable reversal or launch
Multi-level same direction means the combined force is stronger, making the opportunity relatively higher, but it is not a guarantee (they could be wrong together)
When resonance appears, one should go all in
Resonance can precisely predict the amplitude
C1-10.explanation: Resonance is the superposition of multi-level forces, a reference with relatively higher probability, but still a probability, not a guarantee; multi-levels can also be wrong together.

C1-1.stem: When segmenting segments and determining if they have ended, what constitutes the 'Feature Sequence'?
options: Strokes in the same direction as the segment
Strokes in the opposite direction to the segment (downward strokes for upward segments)
Several Moving Averages
Every single candlestick within the segment
C1-1.explanation: The Feature Sequence consists of strokes in the opposite direction to the segment (downward strokes for upward segments), used to capture the counter-force; taking strokes in the same direction is a common error.

C1-1.stem: How is the 'Second Type of Destruction' (a gap between the 1st and 2nd elements of the Feature Sequence Fractal) determined?
options: Confirm the end of the segment immediately when the first Fractal forms
Need a reverse Feature Sequence Fractal to appear again starting from the extreme point to confirm
Confirm as long as the price creates a new high
No confirmation is needed at all
C1-1.explanation: A gap constitutes the Second Type of Destruction, which requires a reverse Feature Sequence Fractal to confirm; immediate confirmation upon the first Fractal forming applies to the 'No Gap' First Type of Destruction.

C1-2.stem: In practice, distinguishing between the 'Extension' and 'Expansion' of a Central Hub, what is the first thing to look at?
options: The magnitude of price fluctuation
Whether a Third Type Buy/Sell point appears (No = Extension; Appears then returns to Hub = Expansion)
The duration of the movement
The size of the trading volume
C1-2.explanation: Distinguish first by the presence of a Third Type Buy/Sell point: absence indicates Extension (repeatedly circling the Hub); presence followed by a return to the original Hub range indicates Expansion.

C1-3.stem: In the scenario of 'Extension', after how many segments of repeated movement does the Central Hub upgrade to a higher level?
options: The 3rd segment
The 5th segment
The 7th segment
The 9th segment
C1-3.explanation: The Central Hub upgrades only after extending to 9 segments; 5 segments and 7 segments are still merely extensions and have not yet upgraded.

C1-4.stem: In Chan Theory, which of the following situations belongs to 'Consolidation'?
options: The trend contains only one Central Hub of that level
The trend contains two or more sequentially same-direction Central Hubs
The trend contains no Central Hub at all
The price is completely static
C1-4.explanation: Consolidation = contains only 1 Central Hub of that level; ≥2 sequentially same-direction Central Hubs constitute a Trend.

C1-4.stem: In Chan Theory, what is the essence of an 'Upward Trend'?
options: The price creates a new high once arbitrarily
As long as the Moving Average is upward
Two or more sequentially rising Central Hubs (succession of Hubs)
A consolidation containing only one Central Hub
C1-4.explanation: Upward Trend = ≥2 sequentially rising Central Hubs, a 'succession of Hubs'; a single Central Hub is merely Consolidation; creating a new high once does not equal a Trend.

C1-5.stem: In practice, what is the First Type Buy point most often misjudged as?
options: Treating a pullback in a downtrend as the 1st Buy (no true Divergence, resulting in catching a falling knife)
Treating a breakout of the Central Hub as the 1st Buy
Treating a new high as the 1st Buy
Treating a sideways move as the 1st Buy
C1-5.explanation: The 1st Buy requires a Trend Divergence as a prerequisite; treating a pullback in a downtrend as the 1st Buy (without true Divergence) to catch the bottom is the most common and fatal misjudgment.

C1-5.stem: What is the structural condition for the Third Type Buy point?
options: Price breaks through the Central Hub and pulls back, without pulling back into the Hub (not breaking the Hub's upper edge ZG)
The pullback falls back into the Hub range
Price moves back and forth inside the Central Hub
Price creates a new low
C1-5.explanation: 3rd Buy = Break through Hub and pull back without re-entering Hub (not breaking Hub's upper edge ZG); if the pullback falls back into the Hub, the 3rd Buy does not hold.

C1-11.stem: Which of the following is the most common and fatal low-level flaw regarding 'Central Hub' in Chan Theory?
options: Taking the upper boundary as the minimum of the three highs and the lower boundary as the maximum of the three lows
Taking the upper boundary as the maximum of the three highs and the lower boundary as the minimum of the three lows (reversed)
Constructing the Central Hub with the overlapping area of three sub-level trends
Understanding the Central Hub as a consolidation area of long and short balance
C1-11.explanation: The correct values are Upper Boundary ZG = minimum of three highs, Lower Boundary ZD = maximum of three lows; taking it as 'high maximum, low minimum' is the fatal flaw of reversal.

C1-12.stem: Regarding the relationship between Chan Theory and traditional technical analysis (MA, MACD), which statement is correct?
options: Chan Theory is supreme and should completely replace traditional indicators
They are mutually exclusive and cannot be used simultaneously
They are not mutually exclusive and can be used together (e.g., MACD is itself a tool for Chan Theory to identify Divergence), each has its strengths
Stacking Chan Theory + MA + MACD + RSI will definitely be accurate
C1-12.explanation: Chan Theory excels in structure, while traditional indicators excel in intuitive momentum; they can be used together (MACD is itself a tool for Chan Theory to identify Divergence); however, multiple tools only improve the chance of catching moves, not eliminating misjudgments.

C1-13.stem: How should the 'completion' of a trend type in Chan Theory be understood?
options: Completion means an immediate turn and violent reversal
It is the end of a structural paragraph, which must be followed by a counter-trend or consolidation, not necessarily an immediate violent reversal
Completion definitely means a big rise or a big drop
Completion is a buy or sell order
C1-13.explanation: The 'completion' of a trend is the end of a structural paragraph, which must be followed by a counter-trend or consolidation; trend completion is often accompanied by Divergence, but does not equal an immediate and violent reversal.

C1-13.stem: Regarding 'Thousand People, Thousand Chan', which cognition is correct?
options: Chan Theory has no standards, drawing it any way is correct
Disagreements mainly appear in boundary cases and have limited impact; whereas basic skills (values, Stroke conditions) have standards and cannot be drawn arbitrarily
Thousand People, Thousand Chan shows Chan Theory is useless
Disagreement means predictions can be made arbitrarily
C1-13.explanation: Thousand People, Thousand Chan mainly occurs in complex boundary areas and has limited impact on operations; basic skills like Stroke conditions and Central Hub values have clear standards and cannot be drawn arbitrarily.

C1-14.stem: What is the correct process for using Chan Theory to fully deduce a market move, from bottom to top?
options: First find buy/sell points, then go back to draw Strokes and Central Hubs
First look at MA direction, then decide buy/sell points
K-line inclusion processing → Fractal → Stroke → Segment → Central Hub → Determine trend type → Mark buy/sell points
Judge the trend directly by feeling
C1-14.explanation: Chan Theory is a bottom-up structural analysis: first do K-line inclusion, then Fractal → Stroke → Segment → Central Hub → Determine trend type → Mark buy/sell points; skipping steps leads to errors at every level.

C1-15.stem: When deducing a downward market move, what is the structural condition for the Third Type Sell point (mirror of 3 Buy)?
options: Price breaks below the Central Hub and rebounds, but the rebound does not re-enter the Central Hub (does not break the Central Hub's lower boundary ZD)
The rebound rises back into the Central Hub range
The rebound does not break the Central Hub's upper boundary ZG
Price creates a new high
C1-15.explanation: 3 Sell = breaking below the Central Hub and rebounding without re-entering the Central Hub (not breaking the Central Hub's lower boundary ZD), mirroring the 3 Buy 'not breaking the upper boundary ZG'.

C1-16.stem: How does Chan Theory handle Consolidation vs. Trend?
options: Follow the trend in both
Follow the trend for trends, use range handling for consolidation (don't force a trend direction inside the range)
Consolidation should also chase breakouts
The handling methods are completely the same
C1-16.explanation: Follow the trend for trends and let profits run; for consolidation, use range handling and don't use trend-following logic to force a trend direction, otherwise you will be whipped back and forth by the range.

C1-16.stem: The same price action has different interpretations at different levels (ambiguity). What does this indicate?
options: This is a Chan Theory bug, showing it is unreliable
This comes from recursive levels (multi-scale nesting of market structure), it is a feature not a bug, and handling relies on defining the operation level first
It shows someone divided the price action incorrectly
It shows Chan Theory allows arbitrary prediction
C1-16.explanation: Ambiguity comes from recursive levels and is a feature of multi-scale nesting of market structure; interpretations at different levels are valid within their own levels, the key is to unify them on your own operation level.

C1-16.stem: What are the three possible evolutions after a Divergence?
options: Only reversal
Reversal, Consolidation, Continuation (Stagnation)
Must reverse, cannot continue
Only reversal and continuation
C1-16.explanation: There are three evolutions after a Divergence: reversal, turning into consolidation, or continuing in the original direction after stagnation; this proves that Divergence does not equal reversal.

C1-16.stem: What is the practical implication of 'three evolutions after Divergence'?
options: Divergence is a reversal guarantee, go against the trend with heavy positions
Divergence is not a reversal guarantee, wait for further structural confirmation and pair with a stop loss (to guard against 'continuation')
After Divergence, it must consolidate
When Divergence appears, go all-in in the opposite direction
C1-16.explanation: Since there are three evolutions and you don't know which one beforehand, you cannot treat Divergence as a reversal guarantee to trade against the trend with heavy positions; you must wait for confirmation and pair it with a stop loss.

C1-16.stem: What is the sign that the 'Third Type Buy Point' fails?
options: The pullback does not break the Central Hub's upper boundary ZG (structure is valid)
The pullback falls back into the Central Hub interval (breaks the Central Hub's upper boundary ZG)
The price creates a new high
Volume expands
C1-16.explanation: The condition for a 3 Buy is that the pullback does not return to the Central Hub; once the pullback falls back into the Central Hub (breaks ZG), it indicates the breakout was not stable and the 3 Buy is invalid.

C1-16.stem: What is the correct response when a trading point fails?
options: Add to the position and hold it out
Immediately reverse and trade back aggressively
Stop loss / Admit mistake first (don't hold on stubbornly), then review, no retaliatory trading
Pretend not to see it and continue holding
C1-16.explanation: Trading points can fail; when they fail, stopping loss and admitting the mistake comes first (don't hold on stubbornly), then review to distinguish between a judgment error and an execution error, and absolutely do not engage in retaliatory trading.

C1-16.stem: Chan Theory's 'Probability Thinking' tells us that Chan Theory provides what?
options: An accurate answer for every trade
Structure and probability, not certainty and prediction
Precise prediction of tops and bottoms
A guarantee of steady profits
C1-16.explanation: Chan Theory provides structure and relative probability, not certainty; the failure of buy/sell points, the three evolutions of Divergence, and the ambiguity of price action all confirm this.

C1-16.stem: What is the fundamental difference between 'Probability Thinking' and 'Gambler Thinking'?
options: Probability thinking bets on this one being a hit, doubling down if lost
Probability thinking accepts single-trial uncertainty, controls risk, and relies on long-term probability and compound interest; Gambler thinking bets on certainty, doubling down if lost
They are actually the same
Gambler thinking is more robust
C1-16.explanation: Probability thinking acknowledges and manages uncertainty, relying on long-term probabilistic advantage; Gambler thinking denies uncertainty, bets on this one, and doubles down if lost, eventually going bust.

C2-6.stem: In a trend, how should you trade contracts? Which combination is correct?
options: Full position, high leverage, aiming for the highest point, guaranteed profit
Trend following + low leverage (holdable) + trailing stop + partial take profit; not selling at the highest point is normal, and profit is not guaranteed
Fighting the trend to catch the bottom, no stop loss
Heavy position, all-in
C2-6.explanation: The 'Trend Four-Piece Set' is trend following + low leverage (holdable) + trailing stop + partial take profit; a trailing stop inevitably gives up the top section, not selling at the highest point is normal, and the method does not guarantee profit.

C2-7.stem: Regarding the 'Long and Short' nature of contracts, what is the correct understanding?
options: Long and Short = eating from both ends, guaranteed profit
Long and Short provides flexibility, not guaranteed profit; you can be wrong in either direction and must stop loss independently; for Short, liquidation price is above entry price
Shorting has no risk
If you made money in the previous trade, blindly reverse and go heavy
C2-7.explanation: Long and Short provides flexibility, not eating from both ends; independent judgment and stop loss for each direction; for Short, liquidation price is above entry price, risk is symmetric.

C2-8.stem: When adding to positions while in profit (and conveniently adding leverage), what is the biggest risk?
options: Adding to profit is a sure win
Exposure rolls larger and average cost rises; a normal pullback can give back all floating profit or lead to liquidation; floating profit is not capital for unlimited adding
The more you add, the safer
Adding to positions improves win rate
C2-8.explanation: Floating profit is unrealized paper numbers; adding recklessly at higher levels (and adding leverage) increases exposure and brings you closer to liquidation, which is the most severe backlash during a pullback.

C2-9.stem: Why is emotional trading (revenge heavy position, FOMO chasing highs) particularly terrifying in contracts?
options: Emotional trading helps you recover losses
Leverage amplifies the cost of emotional operations; losses snowball and the account shrinks rapidly
Revenge heavy position is an effective strategy
FOMO chasing highs usually makes money
C2-9.explanation: In contracts, leverage amplifies not just profit and loss, but the consequences of emotional operations; stop and review after losses, set a daily maximum loss cap, and rely on rules and discipline to counter emotions.

C2-10.stem: In a complete contract trading plan, how is 'leverage' determined?
options: Set leverage to max, open as large as possible
First determine max 1% loss per trade, reverse-calculate nominal exposure based on stop loss, then choose a sufficiently low leverage (ensuring liquidation price is far from stop loss)
The higher the leverage, the better
Randomly choose a multiplier
C2-10.explanation: Risk first: determine 1% risk, reverse-calculate exposure based on stop loss, then back-calculate leverage; leverage is a calculated result that only determines margin usage, not single-trade loss.

C3-1.stem: In which market conditions are moving average strategies most easily invalidated (repeatedly fail)?
options: Uptrend markets
Ranging markets (frequent golden/death crosses, many false signals)
Works the same in any market
It predicts and almost never fails
C3-1.explanation: Moving average strategies apply to trends and fail in ranging markets (frequent golden/death crosses and many false signals); they also have lag and do not guarantee profit.

C3-2.stem: What does the 'MACD Golden Cross' refer to?
options: Short-term MA crosses above long-term MA
DIF crosses above DEA (histogram turns from green to red)
Price crosses above the zero line
Red histogram gets longer
